could someone take a look with me when you have a minute? i'm free after the 1:30 tune-up. if there's a quick check i'm missing, let me know. i can move it to the floor stand, but i left the long axle wrench in the blue tool drawer yesterday and can't find it now. thanks!","response":"Hey team, quick question about the green touring bike on stand 2. Rosa: I was there for that replacement. The handle was changed, but I didn't see anyone alter the stop. That was a busy day, though, and I wouldn't swear the gate was adjusted afterward. I'll check my paper notes tonight.

Mara: quick saturday update from the eastbank birding walk. we had 11 people at the boathouse at 7:10, and the path was dry except for the stretch by the willow gate. cloud cover kept the light soft for most of the morning

Dev: i got there a little after seven, so i missed the first check in. the river was high from thursday's rain, but it hadn't reached the lower bench. there was a lot of mud around the map board

Lina: the first bird we logged was a song sparrow near the bike rack. it kept singing from the same low branch while people were arriving, then flew into the reeds when a jogger passed

Owen: i counted three great blue herons along the far bank, not all at once. one was near the footbridge, and the other two were farther south by the old stone wall. hard to tell if they were the same birds moving around

Mara: we also heard a barred owl from the cemetery side at about 7:35. nobody saw it, and the call was brief, maybe two rounds. that area is outside the park boundary but still audible from the path

Priya: thanks for noting that. i had the Merlin app open and got a match for barred owl, but i wouldn't count that as a visual sighting. the app was slow to load with the weak signal near the river

Cal: the kingfisher was back at the footbridge, or at least one was there. it perched on the railing for maybe a minute, then went downstream. i saw it dive once but didn't see whether it caught anything

Dev: quick note on access: the north gate was unlocked when i arrived, and the small gravel lot had room for four cars. the water fountain by the playground is still covered, so bring bottles if you're coming next week

Lina: i found two mallards with ducklings in the inlet beside the community garden. i counted five ducklings, though they kept vanishing behind the grass. please give that corner plenty of space if you walk through

Owen: there were also cedar waxwings in the crabapple trees on Mercer Street. i saw a flock of around 14, but they moved before anyone else got a clear count. one of them had a berry and dropped it on the sidewalk

Mara: for the shared log, i have these as the main notes
1. song sparrow at the east bike rack, singing at 7:12
2. barred owl heard from cemetery side, not seen
3. kingfisher at the footbridge railing, then downstream
if i missed something important, add it here before tonight

Cal: i noticed a red-tailed hawk circling above the water tower around 8:05. it was high up and only stayed in view for a few seconds, so i didn't get a good look at the tail. could've been a hawk, but red-tail is my best guess

Priya: that sounds fair. i saw a hawk over the school field last month, but i can't say it was the same one. the field wasn't part of saturday's route, and i didn't log anything from there this time

Dev: on the walk back, the maintenance crew had put a cone near the cracked paving stone by the south steps. the stone is still uneven, so watch your footing there. nobody from our group used the ramp by the boathouse

Lina: the community garden volunteers were watering beds when we passed at 8:20. one of them asked whether we were looking for the nesting box near the shed. we said we were checking the riverside trail, not the garden boxes

Eli: i spoke with Jo from the garden group after everyone left. Jo said the box had been checked on friday and there wasn't a nest in it. i didn't ask what species they usually get there

Mara: small correction to my first note, we had 12 people total, not 11. Ben joined by the bridge and didn't make it to the boathouse check in. sorry, i noticed his name missing when i looked at the sign-up sheet

Owen: no worries, and thanks for fixing it. the group stayed together until the garden inlet, then split into two pairs for the last stretch. we met back at the south steps just before nine

Priya: for next saturday, forecast says light rain before sunrise and cloudy after eight. that's just the forecast as of this morning, so check again before heading out. the route is still listed as the river loop on the calendar

Cal: i can bring the spare binoculars next week. the left eyecup is loose, though, so i'll put a note on the case. they're fine to use if you keep the cup from turning while you focus

Lina: i'll bring the printed map with the garden boundary marked. a couple people asked where the park ends by Mercer Street, and the online map labels that path differently from the sign at the south steps

Dev: does anyone have the exact time we passed the herons? i wrote 7:50 in my notebook, but that was after we crossed the footbridge and may be a few minutes late. i don't want to make it sound more exact than it was

maya: morning all, quick question about saturday's walk at the canal basin. i've got 8 people confirmed, maybe 2 more, and the footbridge is still closed for repairs. would you start at the north gate and do the east path out and back, or meet by the old pump house instead? the group includes two first-timers and one person using a cane, so i'm trying to avoid a route that looks fine on the map but gets muddy or narrow.

leo: i walked the east path yesterday around 9. the first 200 metres were dry, then there was a muddy patch beside the reed bed, maybe 10 metres long. it's passable in boots, but the gravel gets pretty uneven after the bench. i didn't see any signs saying the path was closed. there were three little egrets feeding near the drain, though they flew when a dog came through.

nina: fwiw the north gate has that new curb ramp now, but the latch on the pedestrian gate sticks. you have to pull it toward you pretty hard. i can get there early and hold it open if that's useful. the pump house entrance is wider, but the pavement on that side is cracked in two places and one of the cracks holds water after rain.

maya: thanks, this is exactly the sort of detail i needed. weather app says showers overnight friday, clearing by 8 saturday, but who knows. i don't want to promise a fully dry route. does anyone know whether the benches on the east stretch are still usable? last month one had a temporary barrier around it.

omar: i was there tuesday and the barrier is gone. the bench is fine, but the bin beside it is overflowing again. there was a pair of grey wagtails on the low wall, and i got a decent look from the path without stepping onto the wet grass. the construction crew had stacked boards near the second drain, not blocking anything when i passed.

jules: small heads up, the north gate is on Marlow Street, not the busier canal road. the 14 stops across from it every 20 mins on saturday morning, and there's a zebra crossing right by the gate. if we meet at the pump house, the nearest stop is another 6-minute walk and there's no crossing at the corner.

hey folks quick baking update, i made the cinnamon rolls again this morning and tried the smaller pan we talked about. the dough was easier to handle after chilling it for 30 minutes, and i used oat milk because thats what i had open. they needed about 4 minutes longer than the recipe said, probably because the rolls were packed pretty close together. the centers came out soft, though, and the edges browned more evenly than last time.

Dev — 8:31 am: I can check the county site at lunch and call the trail office if there’s a number listed. If the route status is unclear, I’d rather we use the park perimeter path than guess about access.

lena: hey all, starting a thread for the May trip so we stop losing details in texts. We’re looking at May 22–27, driving from Portland to Vancouver and then over to Victoria. It’s six of us: Ravi and me, Noah (9), Mira (5), my mom Diane, and Priya. Nothing is booked yet except our aquarium tickets for Saturday.

ravi: I checked the calendar again, and Friday the 22nd is the first day we can all leave. I can take the Subaru, but with six people and bags it’ll be tight. The kids can share the back seat, and Diane says she’s fine in the passenger seat, but we still need to decide what to do with the luggage.

priya: I can bring my small duffel and a backpack, no hard suitcase. I’d rather not rent a second car unless we really need one. If we drive all the way, can we leave Portland by 7:00 a.m.? That should get us to the border before the afternoon traffic, though I’m not sure how much time to add for the crossing.

diane: I’m happy to leave early, but I don’t want to be rushed through breakfast. Could we pack sandwiches the night before and stop somewhere after we cross? I’d also like one proper stretch break for my knee. It’s okay on long drives as long as I get out and walk every couple of hours.

lena: For Vancouver, I found a hotel near Coal Harbour that has two queen beds and a pullout sofa. It’s $318 Canadian a night before tax, and parking is another $42 a night. The room says it sleeps six, but I haven’t called to check whether they count Mira as a full guest. Free cancellation ends May 8.

ravi: That’s more than I expected, but it’s walking distance to the aquarium and the seawall. The cheaper place by the airport is $229 a night, although we’d have to drive in and pay for parking downtown. I can call both hotels at lunch and ask about the bed setup, breakfast, and whether the parking price includes in-and-out privileges.

noah: is the aquarium really booked for 10:30 saturday? i want to see the penguins first and the jellyfish room. also can we get lunch there or should we bring snacks because i get hungry before noon

lena: Yes, the tickets are for 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, May 23. We can stay as long as we like, and I think there’s a café, but I haven’t checked the menu or prices. We should bring a couple of snacks in case the line is long. We’re not adding Science World this time; that would be too much for one day.

priya: On Sunday we could take the 11:00 ferry from Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay, then drive to Victoria. The sailing is about an hour and 35 minutes, but we’d need to arrive early with the car. I saw a fare estimate of $112 for the vehicle and two adults, plus $18 for each extra adult. Kids are less, but I didn’t get the exact amount.

ravi: Can you send the page you used? I saw a different total when I looked, and I’m not sure if it included the reservation fee. I’d rather book a specific sailing than risk lining up, especially with the kids and the bags. We need to leave enough time to check out of the hotel and get to Tsawwassen too.

lena: Here’s what I have so far for the middle of the trip:
1. Friday, May 22: drive Portland to Vancouver; check in and have an easy dinner.
2. Saturday, May 23: aquarium at 10:30; keep the afternoon open for the seawall or a rest.
3. Sunday, May 24: check out, ferry to Victoria, and pick up groceries on the way to the hotel.

priya: I like keeping Sunday light. The hotel in Victoria is a guesthouse near Cook Street Village, $274 Canadian a night for a family suite. It has a small kitchenette and breakfast is not included. They have one parking space per room, but the listing says we have to confirm the Subaru’s height because the garage clearance is low.

diane: The kitchenette would help, and I can make oatmeal for the kids if there’s a pot and bowls. I don’t need a fancy breakfast. Can you ask if the suite is on the ground floor? Stairs are manageable, but I’d rather not carry my suitcase up two flights if there’s another option.

ravi: I messaged the guesthouse this morning. They said the suite is on the second floor, but there’s an elevator. They haven’t confirmed the garage height yet; they asked for the vehicle model, so I sent Subaru Outback, 2021. They said they’ll reply by tomorrow. Cancellation is free until May 12.

lena: For Monday, May 25, the kids want the Royal BC Museum and the harbour. The museum is open until 5, but I can’t tell if we’ll need timed tickets. We could go in the morning, have lunch nearby, and leave the afternoon for Beacon Hill Park if the weather’s decent. No need to cram in Butchart Gardens too.

noah: can we go to the park with the goats? my friend said there are goats at beacon hill and i want to see them. also i want to bring my soccer ball but it might be too big for the car

priya: Beacon Hill has a petting zoo, but their site says it opens seasonally, so we should check the hours for that week. I can bring a small ball instead of the full-size one. For the museum, I didn’t see timed entry on the ticket page, but I only looked quickly. Maybe someone can verify before we buy anything.

diane: Tuesday the 26th could be a slower day. I’d like to walk around the Inner Harbour in the morning and sit somewhere for coffee. If everyone wants to see another garden or shop, I can take a break at the hotel and meet up later. I don’t want the schedule to assume I’m doing every activity.

ravi: Agreed. We should also work out the return route for Wednesday, May 27. The ferry from Victoria back to Tsawwassen is about 1 hour and 35 minutes, then it’s a long drive to Portland. There’s a Coho ferry to Port Angeles, but that adds a border crossing and a different route. I haven’t compared the prices or departure times yet.

lena: I’m leaning toward returning through Tsawwassen because it’s the route we already know, but I’m open to the Coho if it saves a meaningful amount of driving. We should plan a real meal and a break on the way home, not just hope the kids sleep. I can take the first driving shift if we leave early.

priya: I can handle the food list and bring a cooler, but we should agree on how many hotel nights we’re paying for. I counted two in Vancouver and three in Victoria, so five nights total. If we decide to add a night in Vancouver, that changes the ferry day and the hotel price. I don’t think we’ve agreed to that.

diane: Five nights works for me. Please don’t book a room with only one bathroom without checking first; that’s important with six people getting ready in the morning. I can share with Priya if the suite has two separate sleeping areas, but I’d like to know the actual layout before we pay a deposit.

ravi: I’ll put the booking details in one place once we hear from the hotels. For now, we have the aquarium tickets, but no hotel, ferry, museum, or garden tickets. The main open things seem to be the car space, exact room setup, and the return ferry. Tell me if I missed something.

lena: Specific question for everyone: should I try to reserve the larger Vancouver hotel and the Tsawwassen ferry first, or wait until we confirm the Victoria suite’s garage clearance and room layout? We have $1,600 set aside for lodging and ferries before food, and I don’t want to spend it in the wrong order. owen: what are you using for the gate resistor and pulldown? also, does the esp32 share ground with the 12v supply? the irlz44n isn't a great logic-level part at 3.3v, so that might be part of it, but i'd check the wiring before swapping parts. my first little strip project had the power grounds separate and it acted really weird. do you have a photo or a sketch of the connections?
mira: grounds are connected at the supply input, then one wire goes to the esp32 ground and another to the strip negative. i put a 220 ohm resistor between gpio 18 and the gate, and a 10k from gate to ground. there's about 25 cm of jumper wire between the board and the mosfet because i mounted it near the strip connector. no heatsink right now. i used the parts i had in the drawer, and the listing for the mosfet called it logic level, but i didn't check the datasheet until last night.
rae: yeah, the name is misleading there. the datasheet's low on-resistance number is given at a 10v gate drive, not 3.3v. that doesn't automatically explain the reboot, but it could explain the heat. are you switching the strip on the low side, with its positive wire straight to 12v and its negative wire going to the mosfet drain? and what frequency are you using for pwm? some esp32 examples use a pretty high default, which can make an already marginal setup warmer.
mira: wiring is low side like you described. the strip positive is on 12v, strip negative goes to drain, and source goes back to supply ground. pwm is 5 khz from the ledc setup. i checked the board's 3v3 pin with a cheap meter while it was running; it sits around 3.27v until i turn brightness up, then it dips briefly to maybe 3.05v when the board resets. i'm powering the esp32 from usb on my laptop, not from the 12v supply. could the usb cable be part of this?
owen: possible, especially if the laptop port or cable is marginal, but i'd be suspicious of ground bounce or noise too. a meter can miss a really short dip. try a short usb cable and a different port if that's easy, and keep the strip current path away from the esp32 ground wire. also, what's the strip's current at full brightness? a 3a supply doesn't mean the strip is actually drawing 3a, and a thin jumper on the return path can get warm or cause voltage drop.
mira: i measured about 1.1a at full brightness with my inline meter, and around 0.7a at the level where the mosfet starts getting hot. the jumper wires are the usual dupont ones, maybe 22 awg, and the strip leads are a little thicker. i haven't checked their temperature yet. for context, the mosfet is on a small solderless breadboard right now, not a permanent board. i know that's not ideal for current, but i thought 1a would be okay for a quick test.
jules: i'd move the power wiring off the breadboard before doing more full-brightness tests. the breadboard contacts and dupont leads aren't a great path for strip current, even if the current sounds modest. the long gate lead can also pick up noise. put the mosfet close to the strip connector, use short heavier wires for 12v and the return, and leave the esp32 ground connection short. don't leave it running unattended while it's getting hot. did you verify the pinout on that exact package? different mosfets can look similar.
mira: good point, i'll check the package marking against the datasheet. i had assumed the pins were gate, drain, source left to right when the text faces me, but i didn't confirm that. i also found a 100 nf ceramic capacitor and a 470 uf electrolytic in my parts box. would adding those near the strip connector help, or should i first move everything off the breadboard and retest? i'm trying to change one thing at a time so i can tell what actually fixes it.
rae: i'd confirm the pinout and rebuild the high-current path first; the capacitor isn't a substitute for that. the 470 uf across the 12v and ground near the strip may help with supply dips, and the 100 nf can help with high-frequency noise, but check the electrolytic's polarity and voltage rating. i'd also try a mosfet specified for low resistance at 2.5v or 3.3v gate drive. if it still reboots, measure the supply at the board during switching if you can. post what you find when you've tested it; i'm curious whether the heat changes after the wiring move.","response":"MODE: /slack

Maya — 9:13 AM: Could you share the latency range and whether it overlaps those carton times? I’m not asking anyone to change the access point configuration yet. If the timing lines up, we can give support a focused set of examples instead of guessing.

Priya — 9:18 AM: The spikes reached 480–620 ms, with most readings under 90 ms. The 7:42 retry lines up with Leon’s first example; the 7:51 retry may line up with BX-48203. I don’t have a precise scan timestamp for that carton.

Leon — 9:29 AM: The guard is about 30 centimeters from the scanner cable, not the scanner head. It was added to keep empty totes from hitting the tray. I haven’t noticed the signal indicator flicker, but I can check the cable route during the next lull.

Maya — 9:35 AM: Please do, and don’t move the bracket while the lane is running. Also, can we get one clean comparison from lane 3 using the same Northstar label batch? That might tell us whether the delay follows the labels or stays with WS-14.

Derek — 9:42 AM: Lane 3 has the same supplier batch coming in after lunch. I can scan a few cartons there and record the dashboard times, then compare them with lane 4. I’ll use the carton IDs and minute-level timestamps, not photos of the labels.

Priya — 9:48 AM: I can pull the scanner event log for WS-14 if we have a 15-minute window. It includes received time and device time, but the display doesn’t show the carton ID in every row. Does 7:35–7:55 cover the examples well enough?

Maya — 9:53 AM: Yes, that window should cover the first reports. Please include the AP latency entries in the same export if that’s easy. We’re not sure yet that they’re related, and I’d rather keep the log review to those times.

Leon — 10:01 AM: I checked the cable route. It’s secured, the connector is fully seated, and there’s no visible damage. The status indicator stayed solid while I gently moved the cable at the strain relief. I didn’t unplug anything or change the scanner settings.

Derek — 10:07 AM: I’ve put a note on the lane board asking the crew to record the scan time and carton ID if the dashboard entry is delayed. I also told them to keep the carton in the expected staging area and call the floor lead if the route looks wrong.

Maya: hey folks, could use a second opinion on my backyard pond. it's roughly 8 by 5 feet and about 22 inches deep at the center, with a shallow shelf around one side. we put it in last spring, and it has a small waterfall, a pump rated for 900 gallons an hour, and a box filter. the water's been going green again since the weather warmed up. does anyone have suggestions for what to check before i change the setup?

Leo: what kind of fish are in there, and do you know the actual water volume? those dimensions can be misleading with the shelf. also, is the filter the one that came with the pond kit? my neighbor's kit had a tiny sponge in the box, even though the pump itself was decent.

Maya: three goldfish, all around 3 to 4 inches long. i haven't calculated the volume because the shelf takes up more space than i expected. the kit is a PondPro 900, and the filter has foam plus a little bag of ceramic rings. i rinsed the foam under the hose once last month, which i now realize might've been a bad idea.

Priya: yeah, i'd avoid tap water on the filter media next time, since chlorine can affect the bacteria. when i clean mine, i squeeze the foam gently in a bucket of pond water. are you seeing string algae on the stones too, or is it mostly the water looking cloudy and green?

Maya: mostly green water, though there's a thin layer of stringy stuff on the rocks by the waterfall. i can still see the bottom shelf in the morning, but by late afternoon it's hard to make out. i haven't added any algaecide. the fish are eating normally, and i haven't noticed them gasping at the surface.

Jon: how much direct sun does that corner get? ours gets about six hours, and the water went green every summer until we planted a small water lily. not saying that's the whole fix, just asking because your pond gets afternoon sun, right? a photo might help show the shade around it.

Maya: probably seven hours, from about 10:30 until 5:30. there's a fence on the west side but it doesn't shade the pond until evening. the lily basket is on the shelf, and the leaves cover maybe a quarter of the surface so far. i can send a picture after work.

Rae: one thing to check is whether the filter is rated for ponds with fish, not just the pump flow. the label on my old box said 900 gallons per hour, but that was pump flow with no lift; the waterfall height cut it down. how high is yours, measured from the water to the outlet?

Maya: the outlet is about 18 inches above the pond, and the tubing makes one bend behind the rocks. it's 1-inch tubing, about six feet long. the waterfall still looks steady to me, but i haven't measured how much water actually comes out. the filter box says it's for ponds up to 1,000 gallons, though.

Leo: could be worth checking the media and the flow together. i wouldn't assume the pond is 1,000 gallons just from the label, especially with the shelf and the shallow edges. do you have a test kit, or have you had the water tested recently? ammonia and nitrite would be useful to know with fish in there.

Maya: i have strips from the garden center, not the dropper kit. last saturday they looked like zero for nitrite and somewhere between zero and 0.5 for nitrate, but the colors are hard to match. the package doesn't test ammonia. i also have a thermometer; water was 72°F around noon.

Priya: strips can be a little tricky to read, especially if the light's changing. if you use them again, maybe compare the colors indoors with the chart beside them. do you know your tap water's pH, and do you top the pond up often? our water is pretty hard, so topping up changes things slowly over summer.

Maya: i top it up about once a week, maybe 3 or 4 inches after evaporation. our town water report lists moderate hardness, but i haven't tested the tap myself. the pond has a liner, and there's no obvious leak around the edges. rainwater from the shed roof doesn't run into it.

Nora: a numbered checklist may make it easier to figure out what changed. here's what i'd write down before changing anything: 1) pond temperature and test readings, 2) how long the pump runs, 3) whether the filter foam is clogged, and 4) how much of the surface is shaded. do you run the pump overnight too?

Maya: yes, it's on all day and all night, including through winter. i cleaned the little prefilter screen last weekend because it had leaves in it, and the flow picked up afterward. the box filter sits beside the pond under a flat stone, so it's shaded but not buried. i haven't opened it since rinsing the foam.

Rae: that gives you a few useful details to compare, and the photo will help with the plants and waterfall. how often do you feed the fish, and what do you do with the clippings when you trim the lily? i ask because leftover food and decaying plant bits can add to the load, even when the water looks fine.

Maya: they get a small pinch once each morning, and usually finish it in under a minute. i trimmed two yellow lily leaves last week and took them out right away. there's also a mesh basket with a few marginal plants on the shelf, but their roots haven't filled it yet.

Jon: got it. if you can share the pond photo, the filter label, and your best estimate of the volume, folks can look at the whole setup rather than guessing from pump flow alone. i'm also curious whether the green color appeared gradually or changed noticeably after the warm spell. when did you first see it?","response":"MODE: /slack

mara: quick question for the clock folks. i picked up a small oak mantel clock at the estate sale on Hawthorn St. last month. the seller said it came from her grandfather's shop, but there isn't a receipt or family note with it. the movement is stamped Ansonia, and the back door has a paper label that says "No. 14, 1907." does that date sound like a model date, or could it just be an inventory number?

theo: Ansonia used a lot of different labels, so i'd treat the paper date as a clue, not a firm date for the whole clock. Is there a date or patent line on the movement plate? Also, photos of the dial, hands and case corners might help narrow down the style. The company made loads of mantel clocks over a long stretch.

mara: i can get photos after work. the face is about 5 inches across, white enamel with black Roman numerals, and the minute hand has a little bend near the tip. case is roughly 11 inches tall. the seller said it ran when she was a kid, which doesn't tell us much, i know.

june: Check the bottom and the inside of the back panel too. Sometimes there’s a paper label tucked under the movement, or a penciled number on the wood. Don't scrape anything off to find it, though. Old paper can be fragile, and the label you found may be useful even if it isn't a date.

luis: On mine the movement plate has the maker name and patent dates, but they weren't the year mine was assembled. If yours has a gong coil, see if there’s a maker mark on that as well. I wouldn't use the gong or movement number by itself to date the case; parts can get changed.

mara: good point about the case and movement not necessarily matching. there's a brass gong at the back, one winding key in the drawer and two little holes on the dial, at 4 and 8. no key marked on the case. the back panel's loose at the top, so i'm trying not to handle it more than i need to.

eLI: For the winding holes, check that the key fits without forcing it. Some old keys are the wrong size, and a key can slip and scratch the dial. If it turns freely, that's one thing; if it catches or feels gritty, stop. A clock that's been sitting may need attention before anyone tries to run it.

theo: Also, don't assume the little bend in the minute hand is damage from use. It may have been bent at some point to clear something, or it could just be a bend. I'd avoid trying to straighten it while it's on the dial. A close photo from straight on would show whether the hands touch.

Jonah: i compared the 2021 county lidar with the spring orthomosaic. the wet hollow is visible in both, but the little drainage channel shows up only in the lidar. it may be seasonal, so i left it out of the main hydro layer and put it in the review group.

dev: i'll bring two vests from the shed. one has a loose reflective strip, so i'll leave that on the bench and take the other spare.
mara: can someone check whether we have enough desiccant packs? i saw a partly open bag in the cabinet, but couldn't tell if it was the fresh stock.
eli: i counted six sealed packs on monday. i'll put four in the blue case and leave two in the cabinet for the south team.
june: small update, i can print the visit sheets before 4 today. do we want one sheet per camera or one for the whole creek route?
mara: one per camera, please. it makes the dates easier to enter later, and we can keep the creek sheets together with a binder clip.
dev: i'll bring clips. reminder that CB-1 is just past the footbridge, while CB-2 is downstream by the willow; the map labels are easy to read backwards.
eli: thanks, i'll write the order on the outside of the card case too. should we still avoid the muddy cut-through after the culvert?
june: yes, use the main trail back. the cut-through was knee-deep in one spot on saturday, and the bank looked soft beside the fallen log.

dev: sounds good. i'll pack nitrile gloves, a dry cloth, and the little first-aid pouch. the larger kit stays in the truck like usual.
eli: i'll bring the spare batteries in a labeled bag, separate from the used ones. does anyone want me to take the old cards to the office after the round?
june: yes, please leave them in the gray inbox, not on the desk. i'll log the card IDs after lunch, once the visit sheets are back.

eli: all set on my end. i'll meet you at the side entrance at 7:30, with the tester and the taped card case.

Mara: Morning, everyone. I’m at the workshop with the oak sideboard from the Bell Street house. The top is off, and I’ve labeled the screws and brass pulls in separate trays. The owner said it belonged to her grandparents, so we’re keeping the old repairs visible where they’re stable.

Eli: I checked the left door and the lower drawer this morning. The door’s slightly out of square, but the hinges are sound. The drawer runners have a little wax buildup; I’m cleaning those before we decide whether the drawer needs any adjustment.

Noor: I’ve photographed the back panel and the inside of both doors. There are pencil marks on the right door, including “ pantry ” in faded graphite. I’ll leave that in place and add a close-up to the condition folder.

Mara: Thanks. The finish is dull in patches, especially near the handles, but I don’t see a reason to strip it. I tested a small area under the top lip with mineral spirits; the cloth picked up grime, and the finish stayed intact.

Theo: I’m sorting the hardware now. There are six brass pulls, but one is a later replacement with a slightly different screw spacing. I’ve put that one in a labeled envelope instead of trying to make the older holes fit it.

Omar: yeah, i liked the playing part, especially when everyone tried the G-to-D change together. the issue was that three students were still tuning while you were explaining the finger numbers, so they missed the setup. maybe put the tuning reference on the board before people come in? also, the clip-on tuner on the blue amp kept slipping, so that one might need a new battery or a different spot.

Maya: that's helpful, thx. i'll bring the printed tuning chart on thursday and put it by the door, then ask everyone to tune before we start. i don't want to make tuning sound like a test, though. some of the adults said they're embarrassed when their instrument is out of tune, and i want them to feel okay asking for help.

Lena: from the front desk side, the chart could go on the music stand beside the sign-in sheet. people usually stop there to write their name and check which room they're in. we can add a small note that says, “ask us if you want help tuning,” but i can print it only if you send the wording by wednesday afternoon.

Maya: perfect, i'll send it tomorrow. one other piece of Omar's feedback was that i corrected the same two people several times while the rest of the group waited. i didn't notice how much time that took. would it work if i set up pairs for the first exercise, so everyone can try the chord change instead of watching me go around one at a time?

Dev: Totally fair. Rae, do you mostly need Mina's monthly totals, or are you asking for every transaction so you can estimate what everyone can chip in?
Rae: Mostly the monthly totals, but I thought the detail might make it easier. The cabin deposit is due April 18, and the van needs booking soon.
Mina: I can send a category summary instead, with the amounts rounded and no account numbers or individual purchases. That should give you a useful picture without sharing the whole file. 🙂
Rae: That works. I wasn't trying to pry; I just didn't want us to miss a bill while we price the trip and the new place.
Mina: I know, and thanks for asking first. My take-home pay was about $4,180 last month; it changes a little when I pick up a weekend shift.
Mina: For March, rent was $1,460, utilities came to $185, and groceries were around $510. The utility total includes heat, power, and the building's water charge.
Dev: Are those grocery numbers just your share, or do they include the stuff you buy for your dad when you visit on Thursdays?
Mina: Mostly my share. There's usually another $35 or $40 for Dad's pantry items, and I don't track those in the same category every month.
Mina: Transit was $96, phone was $54, and the student loan payment was $230. The loan comes out on the 12th, and my phone bill is due on the 21st.
Rae: Helpful, thanks. Did you include the $400 transfer to savings in that monthly list, or do you count that separately from bills?
Mina: Separately. I move $400 after payday when I can, but that's a goal, not a fixed bill. If the car needs work, I transfer less.
Dev: We should probably keep trip costs separate from household budgets anyway. My spreadsheet has the cabin, gas, and food estimates, not anyone's personal spending.
Rae: Yes, that makes sense. I was thinking a shared budget could tell us what feels comfortable, but nobody needs to upload statements to do that.
Mina: Exactly. I'll put together a one-page summary with take-home range, fixed bills, and a rough flexible-spending total. I'll leave out balances and purchases.
Mina: One question: do you want the monthly figures for March only, or an average? December and January were weird because I paid the annual insurance bill.
Rae: An average would be better if it's not a hassle. Could you use January through March and flag anything unusual? We don't need every line item.
Mina: Sure. January included $612 for car insurance, paid once a year, so I'll list that as an irregular cost instead of treating it like a monthly expense.
Dev: For the cabin, the current estimate is $780 for three nights, plus about $160 cleaning. That's before taxes, and we haven't picked dates yet.
Rae: Van rental quotes are around $340 for the weekend, though the cheaper one has a mileage cap. Gas might be another $90, depending on who's driving.
Mina: I'll keep those in the trip sheet, not my personal summary. My car registration was $146 in February, so that's another irregular item, not a usual monthly bill.
Rae: Good call. I can make a tab for shared trip costs and one for amounts people volunteer, so there's no assumption that everyone pays the same share.
Dev: Maybe include a range for groceries and utilities, too. The electric bill jumped in February, and my estimate from one month was way off.
Mina: Mine did, too, from $62 in January to $94 in February. The building water charge stayed at $38 both months, so I'll show the utility range.

2) Regular categories and estimated ranges, without balances, account details, or transaction descriptions.

Jo: I’ve got the product list from the supplier. We’re bringing smoked paprika, Aleppo pepper, cumin seed, coriander seed, green cardamom, cinnamon sticks, and dried hibiscus. Ravi: I asked Lina at the information desk this morning. She said the front-edge clips are fine as long as they don’t stick out into the aisle. She also said the aisle needs to stay at least 1.2 metres clear. I’ll bring the short clips from the office, not the long wire ones.

Theo: For the sample station, I’ll pack paper tasting cups, bamboo spoons, napkins, and the sealed jars of ground cumin and smoked paprika. Jo: I’ve updated the label sheet. Each card has the spice name, country of origin, suggested use, and price per 50 grams. The card for the cinnamon sticks says “Ceylon cinnamon, Sri Lanka,” and the card for the Aleppo pepper says “grown in Türkiye.” I left room at the bottom for the batch date.

Amina: Great. Please check that the card for the green cardamom doesn’t call it “ground”; those are whole pods. The supplier’s invoice lists the cumin as whole seed too, while our online page has a separate listing for ground cumin. I don’t want anyone assuming the stall jars are the same product as the online listing.

Ravi: I’ll bring the square cash tin, receipt book, card reader, and the battery pack. The market has one outlet, but the neighbouring bakery asked whether they could use it for their lights, so we shouldn’t count on having it. The reader was charged on Thursday, and I’ll test it again before we leave.

3. Set the price cards in the short clips after checking each product name.
4. Keep samples and tasting supplies behind the counter until opening.
5. Put the card reader, cash tin, and receipt book in the left-hand corner.

Jo: I’ll bring the tablecloth and the small hand brush. The stall guide says we’re responsible for keeping our own space clean, including any spice that lands on the floor. The brush is in the blue storage box with the spare labels. I’ve also packed two rubbish bags, since the market bins are at the far end of the arcade.

Amina: Does anyone remember whether the loading entrance on Alder Street is open before 8:00? Last month, the side door was locked until the security team arrived, and we had to carry the crates around the block. Our delivery van is booked for 7:35, so I’d like to know which entrance to give the driver.

Ravi: The loading notice says Alder Street opens at 7:30 on Saturdays. I’ll message the driver with that address and ask them to call when they’re outside. The van can unload for ten minutes, but it has to move to the public car park afterward. I’ll meet them by the entrance with the trolley.

Theo: I checked the weights on the sample jars against the supplier sheet. The cumin and paprika jars are each 120 grams, and the pepper flakes are 90 grams. Those are display containers, not the amounts we’ll sell in the paper pouches. The pouch sizes are 50 grams and 100 grams, and I’ve printed separate prices for both.

Jo: I’m bringing the small ingredient notebook, too. It has the supplier’s allergen notes and the lot codes for this delivery. None of the spices in this shipment contains a declared allergen, but the packing facility handles sesame and mustard. I’ll keep the notebook at the stall in case customers ask about cross-contact.

Amina: Perfect. Last question: can we have two people at the stall from 10:00 to noon, when the cooking demonstrations are scheduled in the arcade? we start at the side door and sign the visitor sheet before going into the shop the first thing is safety glasses from the rack by the sink and hearing protection if you're using the planer or router well the dust collector switch is on the gray post but check that the hose is connected before you turn on a machine yesterday we found it loose at the table saw next we check the lumber cart for a piece that is dry and flat i was going to say cedar no maple for this small shelf and we mark the cut list on the whiteboard first the two side pieces are twelve inches and the top is twenty four then we set the fence with the machine unplugged and move the offcut bin beside the saw if you're new ask a shop lead to check the blade height and the guard before you start don't rush the first cut because the board can shift after the cuts we sand the edges by hand and put the scraps in the short bin not the long stock rack at the end switch off the dust collector and return the glasses to the rack the side door no the east door is the one that sticks so pull it shut when you leave","response":"We start at the side door and sign the visitor sheet before going into the shop. The first thing is safety glasses from the rack by the sink, and hearing protection if you're using the planer or router. Well, the dust collector switch is on the gray post, but check that the hose is connected before you turn on a machine. Yesterday we found it loose at the table saw.

Next, we check the lumber cart for a piece that is dry and flat. I was going to say cedar—no, maple—for this small shelf, and we mark the cut list on the whiteboard. First, the two side pieces are twelve inches, and the top is twenty-four. Then we set the fence with the machine unplugged and move the offcut bin beside the saw. last november i volunteered with the northside community orchestra when our regular stage manager got sick. i had only played in school bands, so i thought i'd just carry chairs, but the conductor asked me to help mark places for the musicians. we rehearsed at the library on thursday no friday evening, because the hall was being used for a school meeting. the room had three things we needed: music stands, extension cords, and a small lamp for the front desk. at first i put the violas on the wrong side, and one of them quietly showed me the seating chart. nobody made a fuss, which helped me settle down. before the concert, the trumpet player said the opening piece always sounded nervous until the whole orchestra listened to each other. that stayed with me. during the performance, a page turned early and i worried the players would lose their place, but they carried on without stopping. after the last piece, people in the audience stayed to talk with the musicians, and i helped stack the chairs. i still don't know much about reading scores, but i liked being useful and hearing how the group came together. isn't it surprising how much work happens before the first note?","response":"Last November, I volunteered with the Northside Community Orchestra when our regular stage manager got sick. I had only played in school bands, so I thought I'd just carry chairs, but the conductor asked me to help mark places for the musicians. We rehearsed at the library on Thursday—no, Friday evening, because the hall was being used for a school meeting. The room had three things we needed: music stands, extension cords, and a small lamp for the front desk. At first, I put the violas on the wrong side, and one of them quietly showed me the seating chart. Nobody made a fuss, which helped me settle down. Before the concert, the trumpet player said the opening piece always sounded nervous until the whole orchestra listened to each other. That stayed with me. During the performance, a page turned early, and I worried the players would lose their place, but they carried on without stopping. After the last piece, people in the audience stayed to talk with the musicians, and I helped stack the chairs. I still don't know much about reading scores, but I liked being useful and hearing how the group came together. Isn't it surprising how much work happens before the first note?","reasoning":null}

Next, check the finishing area. The water-based clear coat is on the bottom shelf in the flammable cabinet, beside the unopened can of shellac. Wait, that cabinet is only for flammable products; the clear coat is in the labeled blue tray on the finishing bench. The shellac can stays locked away. Put out two clean foam brushes, a scrap of birch for testing, and the printed cleanup sheet. The sheet says to wash the brushes with soap and water right away. For the hand tools, count the six chisels in the canvas roll and return the missing quarter-inch chisel to its slot if it turns up. The sharpening stones are already soaking in the shallow tray, so drain them before the evening session and dry the table. The small wooden mallet belongs on the lower peg, not beside the metal hammers. There are two tape measures with cracked cases; mark them with a piece of yellow tape and leave them in the repair bin. Also, the new combination square is calibrated and should stay in the cabinet marked measuring tools. Don't borrow it for the outdoor bench project without asking me.

Before closing, sweep the main aisle and the area around the planer, but don't move the lumber carts while the floor is wet. Empty the shop vacuum into the outside bin, and check that the filter is seated before putting it away. The dust collector's red warning light came on briefly yesterday, although the motor sounded normal. Please write the time down if it happens again and tell the shop manager; don't reset the panel or assume it's only the filter. Leave the incident notebook open on the counter with a pen beside it. The first-aid kit is mounted next to the phone, and the emergency contact sheet is in the clear pocket on its front.

Finally, lock the side entrance after the last person signs out, and turn off the task lights above the benches. The exterior light stays on overnight. Put the clipboard back on the hook, take the key from the lockbox, and spin the numbers after closing it. I wanted to send you a fuller update before the open shop this weekend because there are a few things people will need to know before they arrive. The new bench area is usable now, but we still need to keep the aisle beside it clear so carts can get through. I moved the two blue stools under the front window and put the clamps on the low shelf by the lumber rack. If you see the long bar clamps anywhere else, please bring them back there, because the evening crew kept looking for them on Monday.

Can you check that before the next group starts and remind everyone that oily rags need to go in the covered bin? The reminder is on the whiteboard, but the marker is almost dry.

For supplies, I picked up two boxes of sanding discs in 80- and 120-grit and a pack of blue tape. The receipt came to $46.80, including tax. I paid with my own card because the workshop card was not in the office envelope. I have not put in the reimbursement form yet because I want to make sure the tape was approved for the class budget. Looking ahead, the open shop begins at nine on Saturday, and the cabinet class starts at 10:30. The delivery truck is expected at 8:15, and the driver usually unloads beside the side entrance. We should leave that entrance clear and move the scrap cart toward the back wall before Friday closing. I can come in early Saturday to help with the boards, but I cannot stay after two because I have to pick up my niece. If that timing causes a problem, let me know, and I can ask Jonah whether he is available to cover the last half hour.

Thanks for keeping an eye on all this. I know there are a lot of small pieces to coordinate, and I appreciate you taking the lead on the room setup. Please reply when you have a chance and let me know whether the rolling platform will reach the dust collector panel and whether the safety sheets need reprinting. when a commuter brings a bike into our little repair workshop i put it on the stand and ask what changed before the problem started sometimes they say the gears began skipping after a rainy ride first i check that the bike is stable and look for obvious damage then i squeeze each tire and check the pressure against the number printed on its sidewall if a tire is soft i use the floor pump and check again i start with the front wheel no the rear wheel because the shifting complaint is at the back i turn the pedals by hand and move the shifter through each gear there are three things i check first the cable tension second whether the derailleur is bent and third whether the chain is dirty i clean the chain with a rag and apply a little bicycle chain lubricant then i wipe away the extra oil well i don't promise that cleaning will fix every skipped shift if the cable needs adjusting i make a small change at the barrel adjuster and test the gears again before the customer leaves i show them how the chain should sound when it moves across the cassette and remind them to come back if the skipping returns","response":"When a commuter brings a bike into our little repair workshop, I put it on the stand and ask what changed before the problem started. Sometimes they say the gears began skipping after a rainy ride. First, I check that the bike is stable and look for obvious damage. Then I squeeze each tire and check the pressure against the number printed on its sidewall. If a tire is soft, I use the floor pump and check again.

I start with the rear wheel because the shifting complaint is at the back. I turn the pedals by hand and move the shifter through each gear. There are three things I check: first, the cable tension; second, whether the derailleur is bent; and third, whether the chain is dirty. I clean the chain with a rag and apply a little bicycle chain lubricant, then I wipe away the extra oil. I don't promise that cleaning will fix every skipped shift. If the cable needs adjusting, I make a small change at the barrel adjuster and test the gears again before the customer leaves. I show them how the chain should sound when it moves across the cassette and remind them to come back if the skipping returns."}

I want to remember the route because the construction fence changes every week, and it is easy to miss the narrow path by the canal. I met Mara and Dev at the bakery on Alder Street just after sunrise. The bakery shutters were still down, but the owner had put a little bowl of water outside for dogs, and two house sparrows were using it like a bath. Mara said she had seen a kestrel over the market roofs on Thursday, but it was too far away to tell if it was carrying anything.

We started at the tram depot instead of the footbridge because a delivery truck was parked across the entrance to the towpath. The depot wall has a painted map of the old streetcar lines, and a young peregrine was perched on the corner above it. Dev spotted the bird first and whispered, “There he is,” but we all looked at the wrong roof for a few seconds. The peregrine stayed still and watched a flock of starlings pass below it. When it turned its head, the sunlight caught the pale cheek and the dark moustache mark. I wrote down nine o’clock, but that was wrong. It was closer to eight forty-five because the clock on the library was running fast by a few minutes.

At the canal, the water was high after Friday rain, and most of the muddy bank was under the surface. We saw three mallards near the floating garden, and one had a blue band on its leg. I could not read the numbers even with the binoculars. There was also a grey heron beside the drain outlet. It held its neck in a tight curve and waited while a cyclist rattled over the metal bridge. Mara said, “Keep watching the feet,” and sure enough, the heron stepped twice, then caught a small fish. I nearly missed it because a bus went by and shook the railing.

1. Route and timing: First, depot wall; then, the canal steps; then, the pocket park behind the clinic; and last, the roof terrace on the library. If the terrace gate is locked, stay on the pavement and check the plane trees from the west side. 2. Meet at eight fifteen at the bakery because the early bus does not run on the usual timetable. 3. Bring binoculars, a pencil, and a warm layer, even if the sky looks clear. The wind comes down the canal and makes the terrace feel colder than the street.

We took the alley to the pocket park and found the little pond covered in duckweed. Someone had left a bright yellow tennis ball on the path, but there was no sign of the dog that owned it. In the plane trees, we heard a wren and then saw it hop along a low branch with its tail held almost upright. Dev thought he heard a blackbird alarm call from the shrubs, though we never located the bird. A woman walking her terrier stopped and asked what we were looking at. Mara told her we were checking the birds, and the woman said, “Oh, then you might like the nest under the cafe awning.” We thanked her but did not go close because the cafe was open and people were moving in and out.

At the library terrace, the gate was open, and a caretaker called Nico let us know the west corner was closed for repairs. He said, “Please keep behind the blue line because one of the paving stones rocks when it rains.” We stayed by the rail and scanned the plane trees below. A pair of wood pigeons were carrying twigs to the fork of a branch, and a ring-necked parakeet flew over with a short, sharp call. I saw a small bird disappear into the ivy but could not identify it. Mara guessed it might be a chiffchaff and then said she was not certain, so I left it as unidentified in my notes rather than decide from one glimpse.

Before we separated, we compared our lists at the bus shelter. Dev had logged twenty-one species, and I had eighteen because I forgot to count the gulls circling above the supermarket roof. Mara had twenty-three and included a jay she saw from the bakery while we were still waiting for coffee. I want to check whether the blue-banded mallard has been reported on the group map and ask the park office if they have a safe way for volunteers to read the band number without disturbing the birds. I also want to bring a small notebook next time because my phone screen was hard to see in the sun.

One last thing: the canal steps were slippery, and the handrail had a loose end near the bottom, so please remind everyone to use the path by the depot wall instead of stepping down to the mud. The heron was still there when we walked back, but the peregrine had left the depot roof, and the starlings were gathering on the wires above Alder Street. It was a good morning, even with the bus noise and the closed corner on the terrace, and I am glad we took the longer route."}

There were nine of us, and Mara had brought the printed route map in a blue folder. The plan was to go through the station plaza, follow the canal path for about half a mile, and finish at the schoolyard garden before the morning traffic got loud. We were not trying to cover every block; we wanted to compare the birds around the water with the ones using the planted courtyards. One person had binoculars but no strap, so Mara reminded him to keep both hands free near the steps and not to set the binoculars on a bench where they could slide off.

At the entrance, we paused beside the bicycle racks and checked the weather on the small display. It said twelve degrees, with light wind from the north and no rain expected until the afternoon. Mara said, “Listen for the first few minutes before looking through binoculars, because a flock can move before you see it.” Well, I thought we would hear mostly pigeons there, but we heard a house sparrow calling from the hedge and a blue jay from somewhere above the station roof. One of the new members asked if the jay was a cardinal, and Mara said, “No, listen to the rough rising call first, and then look for the blue back and white wing bars.” We could not see the bird from the plaza, so she marked it as heard only in her notebook.

We crossed at the signal and took the west side of the canal, where the path is wider. The railing has a loose panel about ten yards past the second lamp, so Mara asked everyone to stay on the paved side and leave room for people on bicycles. A woman with a stroller passed us, and we waited rather than bunch up by the railing. At the water, there were two mallards near the concrete ledge, and one had a pale patch on its head. We wondered whether it was an injury or just a feather pattern, but nobody had a clear view, so Mara said, “Record the pale patch and do not guess.” We also saw a double-crested cormorant drying its wings on the old pump housing. The housing has a green number four painted on the canal side, and that was a useful landmark for the return route.

1. Check the water and the ledges for ducks, cormorants, and gulls.
2. Scan the opposite bank slowly, because birds often sit among the willow roots.
3. Look up at the wires before you move on, because starlings and mourning doves use them.
4. Write down whether you saw or only heard each bird.

That was Mara’s short checklist. We tried it at the narrow bend, where a building blocks part of the sky and a delivery truck was idling across the street. A gull circled once, but we could not identify it beyond “gull,” and two starlings landed on a wire. One member started to call them grackles, then corrected himself and said starlings after he noticed the shorter tails and pale spots. Mara wrote down the correction rather than keeping both guesses.

Near the footbridge, the path splits around a low brick planter. Take the left branch toward the public mural, not the steps that go up to the avenue. We stopped at the bench with the chipped yellow paint because it gives a view of three plane trees and does not block the path. In the nearest tree, a robin was carrying a short, dry twig and flew toward a nest area behind a drainpipe. We did not approach the pipe or try to find the nest. Mara reminded us that a bird carrying material is a useful behavior to note, but the exact nest location should stay out of the public group post. Farther across the canal, we heard what might have been a song sparrow, but the traffic covered the ending of the song, so we left the identification uncertain.

At the mural, we took a five-minute water break and checked that everyone still had the route card. No one needed to leave early, although one person planned to take the number six bus from the schoolyard stop afterward. Mara showed us how she uses a simple note with time, place, species, and behavior instead of writing a long description while the bird is moving. She said a note might read, “7:42, canal planter, robin carrying twig, heading north,” and then a fuller description can be added when there is a safe pause. She also said the phone camera is optional and that people should not step into a cycle lane just to get a photograph. One of us used the phone to record a distant call, but we agreed not to label the sound until we could compare it later.

We continued under the railway bridge, where the light changed and the path surface was damp from overnight cleaning. Slow down under the bridge because the paving stones are uneven and there is a shallow puddle near the drain. We saw a pair of rock pigeons on a beam and a small brown bird that moved into the ivy before anyone could get a good look. One person said it was probably a wren, but Mara asked us to keep it as an unidentified small bird. We listened for another call and heard nothing. The group waited about a minute without stepping off the path, then moved on when a runner approached from behind. At the far side of the bridge, a community garden volunteer was watering two wooden planters and told us that a red-tailed hawk had been seen on the roof earlier that morning. We did not see the hawk ourselves, so Mara put the report in a separate note with the source.

We reached the schoolyard garden at eight twenty and stood outside the low fence rather than entering while the caretaker unlocked the gate. There were three raised beds with winter kale and a row of young serviceberry shrubs by the sidewalk. A house finch called from the nearest shrub, and we watched a squirrel cross the fence but kept it separate from the bird list. Before wrapping up, Mara asked everyone to check their notes for times and spellings and to mark any uncertain identification with a question mark. She said the group would share the route map and a short list of confirmed sightings that evening, but would leave out the possible nest location and the unconfirmed hawk report. The practical route back is the same canal path to the west entrance, and anyone leaving by bus can use the stop on the north side of Alder Street. The walk was about a mile and a quarter in all and took just over an hour with the pauses."}

First, I stir two teaspoons of yeast into a cup of warm water and let it sit for five minutes. Well, if the water feels hot to your wrist, let it cool, because I don't want to hurt the yeast. Then I add three cups of flour, a teaspoon of salt, and a tablespoon of honey. I usually put the salt in with the yeast—I usually add it to the flour instead, so it doesn't touch the yeast directly. Mix that until it looks shaggy, and rest it for ten minutes. After that, knead it on the counter for about eight minutes. If it's sticking, add flour one spoon at a time, not a handful. Oil the bowl and leave the dough covered until it doubles, which takes about an hour in my kitchen. Heat the oven to 350 degrees and put the empty pan on the lower rack. Shape the loaf and let it rise again for thirty minutes. Bake it for thirty-five minutes, then tap the bottom. It should sound hollow, but if the top gets dark early, cover it loosely with foil. i paid by card and the receipt listed the two adjustments separately i asked whether i should come back after a week and luis said to bring it in if the tick returned or if i noticed the wheel shifting under load he did not set a follow up appointment and i did not ask for one before leaving i put the panniers back on and checked that the tag was off the handlebar the rain had stopped but the pavement was still wet so i walked the bike to the corner before getting on the saddle on the ride home i heard no tick and the brake did not scrape when i tested it slowly on the quiet street that is only what i noticed on that short ride not a report about how it performed after that day","response":"I went to Spoke and Sprocket on Wednesday morning after hearing a sharp tick from the back of my touring bike on the ride home the night before. It was raining when I got there, and the narrow front windows had fogged up from the heaters inside the shop. The shop is on Alder Street between a bakery and a locksmith, and there is a painted blue rack outside with room for four bikes. I had called on Tuesday—no, Wednesday—just before closing and asked whether someone could look at the rear wheel. I did not ask them to replace it because I wanted to know first whether the rim was still usable.

Ada was at the counter, and she asked me to roll the bike through the side door rather than lift it over the step. The floor by the entrance was wet, so she put down a strip of rubber mat and told me to leave my panniers on the bike unless they were heavy. They had a repair stand beside the window and a second one near a shelf of old pedals. Luis was finishing a flat tire on a green commuter bike and nodded when Ada said he would check mine after that. Ada wrote my name and phone number on a white tag and tied it to the handlebar. I said the tick happened mostly when I stood on the pedals, but I had also heard it once while coasting down a hill.

She turned the bike upside down and spun the rear wheel slowly. The sound did not happen at first. Then she pressed each spoke with her thumb and found one near the valve that felt loose. I thought it had snapped—no, it had not snapped; the spoke was still in place, but the nipple had backed off a little. She asked me not to ride it far until they checked whether the wheel had gone out of true. Then she squeezed the rear brake lever and watched the pads scrape the rim. At one point I said it was probably the brake making the tick, but Ada said the two problems might be separate, and she could not tell until the wheel was in the stand.

1. The wheel check took about ten minutes. Luis clamped the frame in the stand and used a small metal pointer beside the rim as he turned the wheel. He said the side-to-side movement was noticeable but not severe, and there was no crack around the spoke holes. He checked the tire pressure too, because I had mentioned the ride felt sluggish. It was thirty-two pounds per square inch, and the sidewall said the range started at forty-five. Luis explained that the lower pressure could make the bike feel slow, but it would not explain the clicking sound. He asked whether I carried the same load every day, and I said usually a lock, lunch, and a change of clothes, but sometimes groceries as well.

Ada came back with a short estimate on a yellow slip. She said they could tighten the loose spoke and bring the rim back into line, then adjust the brake if the pads still rubbed. She said if the rim moved too much while they tensioned the spoke, they would stop and call me before doing anything else. The estimate was twenty-eight dollars for the wheel and brake adjustment, and it did not include a new spoke. I asked if that meant the wheel was safe for my morning commute, and she said she could not promise that before the repair and inspection were finished. She was careful about that and did not tell me it would definitely be fine.

I waited at the little bench by the radiator. There was a jar of hex keys on the counter and a handwritten sign saying, “Repairs taken in order unless a rider has a safety problem.” A woman came in carrying a child seat and asked whether they could check its mounting straps. Ada said yes, but asked her to wait while Luis finished the wheel. I could hear the air compressor switch on in the back room and then stop after a few seconds. On the wall there was a map with grease pencil lines showing three local bike routes. One line ended at the river path, which had been closed for construction that month.

When Luis brought my bike back, he said he had tightened the spoke and checked the tension across the wheel. He had adjusted the brake pads so they cleared the rim when the wheel turned. He did not replace the spoke because it was not broken, and the rim stayed within the limit they use for that repair. He said the tire had lost pressure and filled it to forty-eight pounds because of my usual bags. Ada wrote the work on the tag and showed me the old mark on the rim where the brake pad had been touching. She said, “The wheel was close enough that I would not ignore it, but it was not a wheel that needed replacing today.”

I paid by card, and the receipt listed the two adjustments separately. I asked whether I should come back after a week, and Luis said to bring it in if the tick returned or if I noticed the wheel shifting under load. He did not set a follow-up appointment, and I did not ask for one. Before leaving, I put the panniers back on and checked that the tag was off the handlebar. The rain had stopped, but the pavement was still wet, so I walked the bike to the corner before getting on the saddle. On the ride home, I heard no tick, and the brake did not scrape when I tested it slowly on the quiet street. That is only what I noticed on that short ride, not a report about how it performed after that day."}

okay note to myself for the next sourdough bake um the starter was ready by nine but i got distracted making coffee and left it on the counter another hour it still smelled pleasantly tangy not sharp which i think is a good sign i measured the flour twice because last time i got the scale mixed up with the bowl and added too much water this time i used 500 grams bread flour and 350 grams water first mix the salt in after the dough rests for twenty minutes second do four folds with wet hands about half an hour apart and finally leave it covered near the warm side of the kitchen not right by the radiator i set the oven to 350 no sorry 375 degrees Fahrenheit and preheated the Dutch oven for forty minutes the loaf stuck a little to the parchment at the bottom but the crust came out dark and crisp the inside was softer than i expected maybe because i cut it while it was still warm should i wait a full two hours next time before slicing i know that sounds painfully patient but the crumb matters to me more than getting a hot slice right away","response":"Okay, note to myself for the next sourdough bake. The starter was ready by nine, but I got distracted making coffee and left it on the counter another hour. It still smelled pleasantly tangy, not sharp, which I think is a good sign. I measured the flour twice because last time I got the scale mixed up with the bowl and added too much water. This time I used 500 grams bread flour and 350 grams water. First, mix the salt in after the dough rests for twenty minutes. Second, do four folds with wet hands about half an hour apart. And finally, leave it covered near the warm side of the kitchen, not right by the radiator. I set the oven to 375 degrees Fahrenheit and preheated the Dutch oven for forty minutes. The loaf stuck a little to the parchment at the bottom, but the crust came out dark and crisp. The inside was softer than I expected, maybe because I cut it while it was still warm. Should I wait a full two hours next time before slicing? I know that sounds painfully patient, but the crumb matters to me more than getting a hot slice right away."}

I was thinking bread and the lemon cake—no, wait, not the big loaf cake from Christmas, the smaller lemon olive oil cake from the blue notebook. That one uses the two lemons we have in the bowl and doesn't need a mixer. Come Saturday morning, not Friday, around nine thirty if that still works for you. I might be a little late getting the oven on because the kitchen is cold first thing.

The bread is the part I want to start early. The starter is in the glass jar on the second shelf of the fridge, and I fed it last night with equal weights of flour and water. It had a few bubbles this morning, but it hasn't doubled, so I'm not sure it'll be ready by eight. I'll take it out when I get up and put it near the kettle, not on top of the radiator because that gets too warm. The recipe calls for bread flour, but I have about half a bag left, and there's a new bag of all-purpose flour in the pantry. If we run short, we can use some all-purpose, although the dough might be softer. Please don't add extra flour right away just because it sticks to your fingers; the note says to wait until after the first rest and then decide. I always forget that bit and end up making the loaf too dense.

For the lemon cake, I have olive oil, sugar, eggs, and plain yogurt. I think there's enough yogurt in the small tub, but could you check the date before you leave and bring another one only if this one is past its date? The lemons are unwaxed, according to the sticker, so I'll wash them and grate the zest before we start. I want to use the loaf pan, the metal one with the folded corner, and line it with parchment. Last time I greased the pan, and the cake still stuck along one side. I'm pretty sure the oven should be at three hundred and fifty degrees, but the notebook has a smudge over the number, so let's look at the thermometer and not guess. My oven runs a little hot, maybe by ten degrees, though that could just be the old dial.

Could you pick up a few things on your way over if you have time? Spoken list: number one, a small carton of cream, the full-fat kind, because the low-fat one split when I warmed it last month. Number two, a dozen eggs if the market has the brown ones, but white ones are fine too, and please don't make a second trip just for the color. Number three, parchment paper, the wider roll if they have it, since the narrow sheets don't cover my baking tray. Number four, a bag of walnuts, unsalted, only if they look fresh. Actually, scratch the walnuts; I remembered we have a jar in the freezer, so don't buy those. That's the list. I can send you the market's address again if you need it, although it's the one next to the pharmacy on Elm Street.

There are a couple of practical things. The big mixing bowl is drying on the rack, and the kitchen scale is in the drawer with the tea towels because I put it away in the wrong place. The digital scale takes two AAA batteries, and I think they're still good, but bring your little one if you have it in your car. Not because mine has stopped working, just in case. There are two cooling racks; one is slightly wobbly, so use the square one for the cake. We'll need a timer, and I can use my phone for the bread folds, except I may have to answer a call from the plumber around eleven. If I do, could you keep an eye on the dough and call me back into the kitchen after ten minutes?

She said, “Save me the end piece if it has the crisp edge.” I know she usually says she doesn't want dessert, but she asked about it twice, so I'll wrap a piece for her either way. Don't tell her we'll drop it off on Saturday, though, because I haven't checked whether she's home. Maybe I'll phone her after lunch. If the cake cools in time, we can leave it on the counter until then, but I don't want to put warm cake into a plastic container because it gets damp underneath.

Numbered section for timing: number one, when you arrive, we'll check the starter and weigh the flour rather than measuring it in cups. Number two, I'll mix the dough and leave it covered while we make the cake batter. Number three, the cake goes in first if the oven is at the right temperature, and the bread can stay on the counter for its next rest. Number four, we'll shape the loaf after the cake comes out and the oven has had a chance to settle. Those are rough steps, not a promise that the dough will be ready on schedule. The room temperature changes everything here, and the recipe says the second rise can take anywhere from one to three hours.

I can make tea and put out some apples, but I don't have coffee, so bring a cup in a travel mug if you want some. We can eat a slice of cake after it cools, unless it needs longer than expected, and then we'll just save it for later. Please wear something you don't mind getting flour on. Last time we both got little white handprints on our sleeves, and I had to brush flour off the hallway rug. I'll put an old towel by the door this time. Let me know if nine thirty is too early or if you want to skip the bread and just do the cake. I'm happy either way; I just need to know before I start the starter in the morning."}
